scenes.heading: Storage Optimization
scenes.narration: Storage optimization reduces the bytes you keep and read by choosing the right file format, compression, and layout, cutting both cost and query time.

scenes.heading: Levers that matter
bullets: Columnar formats like Parquet and ORC
Compression codecs balance size and speed
Compact small files into larger ones
Tier cold data to cheaper storage classes
scenes.narration: Columnar formats like Parquet and ORC store each column together, so analytical queries read only the columns they need and compress far better than row formats. Compression codecs let you trade file size against decode speed, with Snappy favoring speed and Zstd or Gzip favoring smaller size. Regular compaction merges the many small files streaming produces into larger, efficient ones. And tiering rarely accessed cold data to cheaper storage classes trims cost without deleting anything.

scenes.heading: Row vs columnar storage
scenes.narration: Row-based storage keeps each record's fields together, which makes writing and retrieving whole rows fast and suits transactional OLTP workloads. Columnar storage groups values of the same column together, so analytical queries scan only the columns they reference and achieve excellent compression because similar values sit next to each other. For the wide scans and aggregations typical of a data platform, columnar formats are almost always the right default.

scenes.heading: Optimizing a table's layout
scenes.narration: This OPTIMIZE command rewrites recent data into fewer, larger files, curing the small-file problem that accumulates from frequent writes. The ZORDER clause co-locates rows with similar customer ids so filters on that column can skip more files through data skipping. The VACUUM command then reclaims storage by removing obsolete file versions that are older than the retention window. Together they keep the table both fast to query and lean on storage.

scenes.heading: The small-file problem
bullets: Streaming writes produce many tiny files
Each file adds read and metadata overhead
Query planning slows with too many files
Compaction merges them into larger ones
scenes.narration: The small-file problem is one of the most common storage pitfalls. Streaming and frequent micro-batch writes each produce tiny files, which pile up quickly. Every file carries fixed read and metadata overhead, so thousands of small files are far slower to scan than a few large ones. Query planning itself slows down as the engine must list and consider all those files. The cure is regular compaction, which rewrites the many small files into fewer files of a healthy size, restoring read performance.

scenes.text: Pick columnar formats, compress sensibly, compact routinely, and tier cold data; storage layout is a first-class performance decision.
scenes.narration: Choose columnar formats, compress sensibly for your read patterns, compact files routinely, and tier cold data to cheaper classes, treating storage layout as a first-class performance and cost decision rather than an afterthought.
